youtube.baslik: Case: A Patient Presenting with Sudden Hearing Loss | Lesson 276 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
In a fictional adult case, we assess sudden sensorineural hearing loss step by step: a focused history and red flags, ruling out conductive causes with otoscopy and tympanometry, masked air and bone conduction, applying the 2019 AAO-HNSF definition, same-day ENT referral, and naming recovery on follow-up audiograms.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Chandrasekhar et al., Clinical Practice Guideline: Sudden Hearing Loss (Update), Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery, 2019; Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology; Gelfand, Essentials of Audiology.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we follow a patient with sudden hearing loss step by step, from the moment they walk in to the follow-up audiograms.
We will cover a rapid but complete assessment, urgent ENT referral and how to interpret follow-up audiograms.

maddeler.metin: New tinnitus in the same ear

cumleler: Our case is fictional: a thirty-eight-year-old person comes to the clinic complaining of a blocked right ear.
The complaint began on waking yesterday morning; the night before, both ears were normal.
Tinnitus that was not there before has started in the same ear, and the person is clearly worried about it.
Thinking it was an earwax plug, the person waited a day and used ear drops, but nothing improved.
There is no vertigo, facial weakness, speech problem or sudden headache; the left ear hears normally.
A blocked ear may sound ordinary, but if it is unilateral and sudden, we must always think of sudden sensorineural loss.
Sudden loss in both ears at once suggests systemic or neurological causes and needs a more urgent assessment.
We ask about neurological symptoms such as facial weakness, speech problems, a sudden severe headache or double vision.
These symptoms may point to a life-threatening cause such as stroke.
Marked imbalance and being unable to walk matter for the same reason.
If any of these is present, the person is helped to reach emergency care without waiting for tests and without losing time.
Recurrent attacks of sudden loss may suggest other conditions such as Meniere's disease; this is also written in the referral note.
The assessment starts with a short, focused history: time of onset, side, associated symptoms and red flags.
On otoscopy we look for conductive causes such as impacted wax, middle ear fluid or a perforation.
Tympanometry shows the middle ear status; it helps us tell whether the sudden blocked feeling comes from the middle ear.
In pure-tone audiometry, air and bone conduction are measured in both ears, with the masking needed.
The speech recognition threshold and word recognition score are added when possible; these scores are also used in follow-up.
Being fast does not mean measuring less; an accurate first audiogram is the basis of every later comparison.
In this case otoscopy is normal in both ears; the canal is clear, the eardrum intact, with no sign of fluid behind it.
Tympanograms are type A in both ears; peak pressure and height are within the normal range.
So there is no outer or middle ear problem to explain the blocked feeling.
A blocked ear with normal otoscopy and a type A tympanogram leads us straight to pure-tone audiometry.
Thresholds in the left ear are within normal limits.
Air conduction thresholds in the right ear are between sixty and eighty decibels.
Because crossover can occur in a severe unilateral loss, the left ear was masked for air conduction testing.
We show the masked air conduction thresholds for the right ear with a triangle symbol.
Right bone conduction was also measured with the left ear masked, and it overlaps air conduction; so the loss is sensorineural.
Without masking, responses from the normal left cochlea could show a false air-bone gap in the right ear.
The pure-tone average of the right ear is about sixty-eight decibels; the picture fits a moderately severe loss.
The audiogram is recorded with date and time, because later follow-up measurements will be compared with this first value.

cumleler.yazi: Per the 2019 guideline of the American Academy of Otolaryngology, sudden sensorineural loss develops within seventy-two hours.
cumleler.ses: Per the twenty nineteen guideline of the American Academy of Otolaryngology, sudden sensorineural loss develops within seventy-two hours.

cumleler: The most widely used audiometric criterion is a loss of thirty decibels or more at at least three consecutive frequencies.
Because the person's earlier audiogram is often unknown, the comparison is made with the other ear's thresholds.
In our case, the difference between the ears is fifty decibels or more at all consecutive frequencies; the criterion is clearly met.
In the clinic, sudden losses smaller than thirty decibels are also taken seriously; the definition is a shared language, not a lower limit.

maddeler.metin: Right SRT 65 dB HL, left masked

cumleler: The right ear's speech recognition threshold, or SRT, was sixty-five decibels HL with the left ear masked; it fits the pure-tone average.
The right word recognition score is forty-four percent at ninety decibels HL; this score will also be used to judge recovery.
In the left ear, the SRT is ten decibels HL and the word recognition score is one hundred percent.
On the tuning fork Weber test, the sound goes to the better-hearing left ear; this fits a sensorineural loss.
Tests such as acoustic reflexes and otoacoustic emissions add information, but they should not delay the referral.
As soon as the results are ready, the loss is documented with masked thresholds and speech scores.
Depending on how the clinic works, the ENT physician is notified by phone or through the system; no one waits in the appointment queue.
A written referral note is prepared, and the person is also given a copy.
The person is referred to the ENT physician the same day.
Treatment options and timing are assessed by the physician; the guideline stresses the early period, especially the first two weeks.
The audiologist does not recommend treatment, but clearly explains to the person why delay matters.
The note first gives the date of onset and, if possible, the time; the assessment is based on this timing.
Then it briefly states the side, and whether tinnitus, vertigo or red flags are present.
Pure-tone results are given with masked thresholds, the pure-tone average and the word recognition score; the audiogram is attached.
The otoscopy and tympanometry results show that no conductive cause was found.
The last line clearly asks for a same-day assessment, because the findings fit sudden sensorineural loss.

sahneler.metin: If someone with a blocked ear has normal otoscopy and a type A tympanogram, do not send them away without measuring bone conduction.
cumleler: A clinical tip: keep sudden sensorineural loss in mind for everyone who comes in saying their ear feels blocked.
If otoscopy is normal and the tympanogram is type A, the blocked feeling may not come from the middle ear.
For such a person, do pure-tone audiometry the same day, and always measure bone conduction with masking.
If you find a sensorineural loss, refer to a physician the same day, without putting the person in the appointment queue.
After the physician's assessment, follow-up measurements document recovery objectively.
The red line shows the first measurement of the right ear, and the gray dashed line the healthy left ear.
The orange line is the check two weeks later; thresholds in the low and mid frequencies improved by fifteen to twenty decibels.
The green line is the measurement three months later; total recovery at one thousand hertz is thirty-five decibels.
But thresholds are still clearly worse than the left ear; there is little change in the high frequencies.
The word recognition score also rose from forty-four percent to eighty-eight percent.
Each time, measurements use the same method, the same earphones and the same masking rules.
By the guideline, complete recovery means thresholds return to about ten decibels of the healthy ear, with a similar word score.
Improvement of more than ten decibels that is not complete is called partial recovery.
A change of less than ten decibels is defined as no recovery.
In our case, the pure-tone average improved by about thirty decibels but is not within ten of the healthy ear; this is partial recovery.
The guideline recommends follow-up audiometry at the end of treatment and within six months after treatment ends.
If recovery is incomplete, tinnitus often remains the most bothersome complaint and needs counseling.
Depending on remaining hearing, options such as a hearing aid or CROS systems, which route sound to the other side, are considered.
Sudden loss in one ear can cause anxiety and insecurity; this emotional impact is also addressed in the session.
The guideline recommends looking for retrocochlear causes; choosing imaging or other methods for this is up to the physician.
Keep in mind that in some people, the cause may only become clear during long-term follow-up.

maddeler.metin: Blocked ear: think of sudden loss
Rule out conductive first, mask bone
Same-day ENT; treatment is the physician's

cumleler: With a unilateral, sudden blocked feeling in the ear, we always think of sudden sensorineural loss.
Conductive causes are ruled out with otoscopy and tympanometry; air and bone conduction are measured with the masking needed.
When the loss meets the criterion, the person is referred to an ENT physician the same day; treatment is the physician's decision.
Follow-up audiograms are taken under the same conditions as the first, and recovery is named with the guideline's definitions.
